description: Cyclic Sort exploits arrays whose values are constrained to a known range tied to the array's length (1..n or 0..n-1) by swapping each element directly into its correct index. After one in-place pass, a linear scan reveals missing values, duplicates, and misplacements in O(n) time and O(1) space — beating both sorting and HashSet-based approaches.
important_details: Trigger condition: the problem states values lie in a range like [1, n] or [0, n] where n is the array length. Without that constraint the pattern does not apply.
Core loop: while nums[i] is not already at its home index, swap it there. Use while, not if.
Guard against infinite loops by comparing VALUES (nums[i] != nums[correctIdx]) rather than indices — with duplicates present, index comparison loops forever.
The second pass is where the answer comes from: compare index i against its expected value and collect every mismatch.
The related in-place technique of negating nums[abs(x)-1] as a visited marker solves the same problems without swaps and is worth knowing as an alternative.
other_relevant_details: Amortized O(n) holds because each swap places at least one element permanently into its final position, so at most n swaps occur overall despite the nested-looking structure. The main trade-off to state in an interview: cyclic sort MUTATES the input. If the problem forbids modification, switch to Floyd's cycle detection (for duplicates) or XOR/Gauss-sum tricks (for a single missing value).

variations.variation: Basic Cyclic Sort (Place Every Number at Its Index)
variations.description: Rearrange an array containing 1..n (or 0..n-1) so each value sits at its natural index, using repeated in-place swaps instead of a comparison sort.
important_details: The while loop at each index is essential — one swap may bring in another out-of-place value that also needs relocating.
Advance i only when the current slot is settled; otherwise stay and keep swapping.
Each element is swapped into its final home at most once, which is what keeps the total at O(n).
For 0-indexed ranges use correctIdx = nums[i]; for 1-indexed use correctIdx = nums[i] - 1. Mixing these up is the most common bug.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) amortized. Space: O(1).

problems.name: Minimum Number of Swaps to Make the String Balanced

variations.description: After cyclic-sorting a 0..n or 1..n array, scan once for the index whose value does not match, revealing the missing number.
important_details: For the 0..n range with n+1 possible values but only n slots, skip any value equal to n during the sort (it has no home index).
If every index matches after sorting, the missing number is n itself — handle this after the scan loop.
XOR and Gauss-sum alternatives also run in O(n)/O(1) but do not generalize to the find-ALL-missing variant; cyclic sort does.
Gauss sum risks integer overflow for large n — mention using long or the XOR variant if asked.

variations.description: When several values from 1..n are absent, cyclic-sort the array and collect every index whose value fails to match, producing all missing numbers in one scan.
important_details: Duplicates occupy slots that missing numbers would otherwise fill — the sort naturally leaves those slots holding wrong values.
The output list is not counted against the O(1) space claim, per standard problem conventions.
The negation-marker alternative is often shorter: for each value x, mark nums[abs(x)-1] negative; indices still positive at the end are missing.
Remember to use Math.abs when reading values during the negation-marker pass, since earlier marks corrupted the signs.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) excluding the output list.

problems.name: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array

variations.description: Cyclic-sort the array and collect values that could not be placed because their home index was already occupied by an identical value — those are exactly the duplicates.
important_details: For a single duplicate, you can return as soon as you detect nums[i] == nums[correctIdx] with i != correctIdx.
For all duplicates, complete the sort first, then scan: any index i holding a value != i+1 holds a duplicate of some other value.
This mutates the input. If the problem explicitly says the array is read-only, use Floyd's cycle detection instead (see the Fast & Slow Pointers pattern).
Binary search on the value range (counting elements <= mid) is a third O(n log n) read-only alternative worth mentioning.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) excluding output. Mutates the input array — state this trade-off explicitly.

variations.variation: Find the Corrupt Pair (Missing + Duplicate Together)
variations.description: When exactly one value is duplicated and exactly one is missing, a single cyclic-sort pass plus one scan yields both at once: the mismatched index gives the duplicate (its value) and the missing number (its index + 1).
important_details: There will be exactly one index i where nums[i] != i + 1 — that slot holds the duplicate, and i+1 is the missing value.
This is strictly better than two separate passes or a frequency array, and it is the intended O(1)-space solution.
Alternative closed-form solution: use the sum and sum-of-squares equations to solve for the two unknowns algebraically, but watch for overflow.
The 2D grid version of this problem (values in an n*n matrix) is solved identically after flattening.

variations.description: The hardest variation: find the smallest absent positive integer in O(n) time and O(1) space by cyclic-sorting only values in [1, n] and ignoring negatives, zero, and anything larger than n.
important_details: Only values in [1, n] can possibly be the answer's neighbours — everything else is noise and is skipped during the sort.
The answer is the first index i where nums[i] != i + 1; if no such index exists, the answer is n + 1.
The bounds check nums[i] > 0 && nums[i] <= n must come BEFORE computing correctIdx, or you get an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
This is the classic Hard-rated question that specifically tests whether you understand cyclic sort rather than having memorized it.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) — meets the strict constraint that rules out sorting and HashSet solutions.

problems.name: Smallest Missing Non-negative Integer After Operations

variations.description: A sibling technique to cyclic sort: instead of swapping values into place, mark presence by negating the value at index abs(x)-1, then read off which indices remain positive.
important_details: Preserves the multiset of absolute values, so the original data is recoverable by taking absolute values afterward.
Always read values through Math.abs during the marking pass, since earlier marks flipped signs.
Only works when the array contains no meaningful negatives and no zeros; pre-process out-of-range values first if needed.
Often shorter and less bug-prone than swap-based cyclic sort under OA time pressure — worth having both in your toolkit.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) in two passes. Space: O(1) excluding output.
